subsection.p: Euler’s method is simple because it uses only the slope at the beginning of each step. That simplicity is also its weakness.

exercise.title: What local idea is Euler’s method repeating?

statement.p: The derivative gives y(x+h)\approx y(x)+y'(x)h. In your own words, why does substituting the differential equation y'=F(x,y) turn that approximation into a step-by-step method, and why is using only the slope at the beginning of each step both a strength and a weakness?

hint.p: The new value is the old value plus slope times step. The method is simple because it uses one slope; it is crude because that slope may change during the step.

subsection.title: Step size and accumulated error
subsection.p: Euler’s method makes a small error at each step. Then it uses the approximate point from that step to compute the next slope. So errors do not merely appear; they can accumulate.
For the same problem,
we can approximate y(2) with several step sizes.
The smaller step sizes give better approximations here. This is what we hope for: more, shorter tangent-line steps should trace the solution curve more faithfully.
But there is a cost. Smaller steps require more computation.
while
The tradeoff is familiar from numerical integration:
The word “usually” belongs in the sentence. A numerical method is not magic. If the step size is too large, the method may follow the wrong behavior.

paragraphs.title: A large-step warning
paragraphs.p: It stays positive and decays toward 0.
They alternate signs and grow in size. That is the opposite of the true solution.
The differential equation describes stable decay. The numerical method, with a large step, creates fake instability.

warning.title: Numerical warning
warning.p: A differential equation and a numerical method are different objects. The equation may have one behavior, while a poor step size in the method can produce another.

paragraphs.p: This does not make Euler’s method useless. It makes it honest. We should use it with step-size discipline and with checks against qualitative behavior.

exercise.title: Why can a large Euler step invent false behavior?

statement.p: Smaller steps usually reduce error, but they are not magic. For y'=-4y, a large step can produce growing oscillations even though the true solution decays. In your own words, why is the numerical method a different object from the differential equation?

hint.p: Each Euler point is approximate, and the next slope is computed at that approximate point. A step that is too large can leave the qualitative story of the field.

subsection.p: Euler’s method uses the slope at the beginning of the step. But if the slope changes during the step, the beginning slope may be a poor representative of the whole interval.

This method is also called Heun’s method. It is not the most powerful numerical method for differential equations, but it fixes one clear defect of Euler’s method: it does not rely only on the starting slope.

exercise.title: What extra information does improved Euler use?

statement.p: Improved Euler averages a beginning slope with an estimated ending slope. In your own words, why should that be a better representative of the whole step, and what computational price does the improvement pay?

hint.p: If the slope changes during the interval, the starting slope alone is biased. Averaging uses two evaluations of F per step instead of one.

subsection.p: Euler’s method does not produce a formula like
It produces a list of points:
If we connect those points by straight line segments, we get a piecewise linear approximation to the solution curve. So Euler’s method approximates not only one number, but a whole function.
This distinction matters.

note.title: What Euler’s method teaches
note.p: A differential equation gives local instructions. Euler’s method turns those instructions into a path by repeating one simple idea:

subsection.p: This is enough when no exact formula is available. But sometimes the equation itself contains a hidden integral. In those cases, we can do better than following short tangent steps. We can solve the equation exactly.
The first such equations are separable.

exercise.title: Why is an Euler table an approximate function, not only a number?

statement.p: Euler’s method produces a list of points rather than a formula such as y=1-e^{-x}. In your own words, why should a report of y(2)\approx0.9375 name the method and the step size, and what object is being approximated besides a single value?

hint.p: Connecting the points gives a piecewise linear path. The output is an approximate solution curve, so the method, step size, and interval belong in the answer.
